The last stone of the junior final belonged to Thea, so Pia spent most of the end crouched near the hog line with her brush across her knees, waiting for it.

Thea was fifteen and had been skip of the club's junior team for two winters. She chose every shot: where to aim, how much weight to put on the stone, when the sweepers should work. Pia was twelve and in her first season, and she swept where she was told. She liked sweeping. Through the brush handle she could feel a stone's speed as a kind of hum in her palms, strong while it was running and thin when it was about to die.

The score was tied. One yellow stone sat at the back edge of the rings, and a second yellow sat as a guard a few feet in front of them, a little to one side. Thea had to send her stone curling around the guard and stop it anywhere closer to the center than the yellow at the back. If she did, the final was theirs.

She pushed out of the hack, slid, and let the stone go with a slow turn of the handle. Pia and Callum fell in beside it, brushes raised.

"Off!" Thea called from behind it. "Stay off!"

The stone drifted on, turning gently toward the guard's shadow. Halfway down the sheet the hum in Pia's palms went thin. It was light. It would die short, and short, she was sure, meant losing. She dropped her brush to the ice and scrubbed hard in front of the stone. Callum glanced at her, then joined in.

"Pia, off!" Thea shouted.

The stone carried. It also ran straighter than it had been turning, and instead of bending in behind the guard it clipped the guard's edge with a hollow crack and skidded off toward the side boards. The yellow at the back of the rings stayed where it was, and the other team began to cheer.

Pia waited for the shouting. Instead, after the handshakes, Thea came and stood beside her with her broom over one shoulder.

"It was light," Pia said. "I could feel it."

"It was," Thea said. "It would have stopped a foot or so short of the button. That still beats a stone at the back of the rings." She tapped the ice with the head of her broom. "Sweeping makes a stone go farther, but it also makes it curl less, and I needed all the curl it had. You could feel the weight. I could see the line. Next time, tell me what you feel, and let me decide what it's for."

On the drive home Pia kept her hands in her lap, turning them over, as if the hum might still be in them somewhere. It had been right, she thought. It had only been half of what there was to know.

All afternoon the rain came down,
the air above us warm enough
to keep it rain, the ground and every branch
so cold it froze the moment that it landed.

on anything that held still long enough:
the clothesline first, and then the low wire fence,
and then each twig of the lilac by the back step,

until the yard was drawn a second time
in glass, each line of it doubled,
the mailbox flag in a clear sleeve,
the gate grown a clear beard of ice.

My mother stood beside me at the sink
and said it was the prettiest thing
she knew of, and the costliest,
and did not say which one she meant first.

Toward dark the sounds began:
a crack, a long hush, then a crash
somewhere past the barn, as if the woods
were dropping armloads of dishes.

By morning the sun was out, and the yard
burned so bright I had to squint.
Half the lilac lay across the walk,
its broken ends as pale as bread.

My mother pulled her boots on
and went out with the saw. I stayed
a moment at the window, holding both,
the shine of it and the sound of it, at once,

and then I went to find my gloves.

Every January, when bitter oranges reached the market for their few short weeks, my grandfather bought a whole crate, and for one weekend the kitchen belonged to marmalade.

He called them Sevilles, after the Spanish city. They are too sour to eat out of hand, and their pulp is crowded with seeds. But they are rich in pectin, the substance that makes jam set, and much of it is in the seeds and the white pith under the skin. So the seeds were kept. I halved the oranges and squeezed them; he sliced the peel into thin strips with a knife he had sharpened on the back step; and the seeds went into a square of cheesecloth, tied up like a little sack, that hung in the pot through the whole boil.

The year I was twelve, I decided the business could be improved. I had read that marmalade sets at around 105 degrees Celsius, and I came home from the hardware store with a candy thermometer bought with my own money. My grandfather turned it over twice, the way he turned over most new things, and clipped it to the side of the pot without a word.

When the needle reached the mark, I announced that the marmalade was ready.

"The thermometer thinks so," he said mildly. "Let's ask the marmalade."

He took a saucer from the freezer, where he had put three of them that morning, dropped a spoonful onto it, and waited a minute. Then he pushed the edge of the puddle with his fingertip. It ran back together like syrup.

I pointed at the thermometer. He pointed at the saucer. We boiled it for six more minutes, and this time, when he pushed, the surface folded into small ridges, like the skin on warm milk. Only then did he turn off the flame.

Later, while the jars cooled on the counter and popped one by one as their lids sealed, he explained, or came as close to explaining as he ever did. The thermometer was right about the temperature, he said, but the temperature was only part of it. Some years the oranges were riper and held less pectin; some years the pot was fuller and boiled differently. The saucer paid no attention to any of that. It showed what the marmalade would do once it was cold, and that was all he wanted to know.

I kept the thermometer. I still have it, in the drawer with the cookie cutters. But the next January I put three saucers in the freezer before he asked, and when he pushed the first one with his finger, I leaned in to watch it before I looked at the needle at all.

For its first forty years, the river town of Tarrow was really two towns joined by a staircase. The mills, the wharf, and the railway depot stood on the flats beside the river; most of the houses, the school, and the churches stood on the bluff two hundred feet above. Between them ran the Long Stair, three hundred and twelve wooden steps that every mill hand climbed at the end of a shift and every shopper climbed with a basket. Wagons took the road around the end of the bluff, a mile and a half of switchbacks.

In 1891 a mill owner named Hollis Greer proposed an incline railway: two cars on a steep track up the face of the bluff, joined by a single cable that ran over a wheel at the top. The design needed no engine. Beneath the floor of each car was an iron tank. At the top, the waiting car's tank was filled with water from a reservoir; at the bottom, the other car's tank was emptied into the river. The heavier car rolled down and, by the cable, drew the lighter one up. A brakeman riding in each car controlled the speed.

The town council doubted it. Water was free, Greer argued, and so was gravity; the only costs were the brakemen's wages and the upkeep of the cable. The council agreed to let him build it at his own expense, provided the fare never rose above a penny.

The incline opened in the spring of 1892, and it changed the town in ways its builder had expected and in one he had not. Mill hands rode it home for their penny, and within a few years the flats, which had once emptied at six o'clock, kept their shops open into the evening, because people could now go down after supper and come back up without the climb. Rents on the bluff rose, and they rose most for the houses nearest the upper station.

What Greer had overlooked was the weather. The reservoir at the top was fed by a spring on the bluff, and in dry summers the spring slowed to a trickle. A car that held too little water was too light to bring the other up with a full load. On those days the incline ran half empty or stood still, and the Long Stair, which some had begun to call useless, filled again.

The council's answer, in 1897, was to keep the stair in repair at public cost, a decision that drew complaints about paying for a thing the incline had replaced. The council clerk wrote in the minutes that a town ought to keep "a way up that does not depend on the weather." The incline closed in 1931, when the last of the mills did. The Long Stair is still there.
